In this paper we propose the generation of synthetic small and more sophisticated molecule structures that optimize the binding affinity to a target (ASYNT-GAN). To achieve this we leverage on three important achievements in A.I.: Attention, Deep Learning on Graphs and Generative Adversarial Networks. Similar to text generation based on parts of text we are able to generate a molecule architecture based on an existing target. By adopting this approach, we propose a novel way of searching for existing compounds that are suitable candidates. Similar to question and answer Natural Language solutions we are able to find drugs with highest relevance to a target. We are able to identify substructures of the molecular structure that are the most suitable for binding. In addition, we are proposing a novel way of generating the molecule in 3D space in such a way that the binding is optimized. We show that we are able to generate compound structures and protein structures that are optimised for binding to a target.

## 1658. Comic China: Representing Common Ground, 1890–1945

- Authors: Erin Y. Huang
- Year: 2021
- DOI: 10.5325/complitstudies.58.2.0e-1
- Venue: Comparative Literature Studies
- Countries: US
- Source: openalex
- URL: https://doi.org/10.5325/complitstudies.58.2.0e-1

What is the role of humor in establishing cross-cultural relations between China and the West? How is humor a lens of representing the West's imagined other? Examining the literary and visual deployment of humor in Anglo-American popular culture of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries—including musical comedies, fiction, travel writing, and cartoons—Wendy Gan's Comic China: Representing Common Ground breaks through Edward Said's theorization of Orientalism and argues for humor's humanizing rather than exoticizing tendencies. Exploring texts that were produced in a time of intensifying cross-cultural encounters shaped by Western imperialism and the two world wars, Gan unravels a nuanced history of humor, where the West's relations with China are put on display in a “swirl of contradictory sentiments,” mixing delight and anxiety, desire and contempt, and mastery and humiliation.Asserting that China is an anomaly within case studies of Orientalism, Gan describes how humor opens up an emergent structure of feeling that records Westerners' negotiations with the disjuncture between the Orientalist invention of “China” as the powerful bearer of ancient civilization and a country subject to Western imperialism in the modern era. Through an eclectic selection of theories on laughter and humor—ranging from Thomas Hobbes to Sigmund Freud, from Henri Bergson to Umberto Eco—Gan illustrates the perceived effects of comedy, which range from the expression of arrogant superiority to the social mechanism of rebellious emancipation. Comic China takes on this disparity by drawing attention to popular culture that has received little scholarly attention, excavating the affective textures of a sentiment and rhetorical device that is seen as increasingly scarce in postwar and contemporary representations of China. Emphasizing humor's contingent and fluid social functions, the book traces the constellation of historical events that shape the ever-shifting relations between the East and the West, and pioneers the study of an affective history constructed upon the translation of emotions across cultures.To illustrate the heterogeneity of Sino-West relations, the book is divided into five case studies. The first two delve into comic representations of China where the “Far East” thrives as the utopian fantasy of a distant land without actuality; the remaining chapters focus on select authors' works that illustrate a bifurcated “China,” coexisting as the “brute reality” of cultural differences and the locus of dreaming for a common ground. Excavating the richness of “China” as the West's imagined other, not reducible to the menacing Yellow Peril stereotype, the first chapter examines chinoiserie in British theatrical productions from the seventeenth to the nineteenth centuries and musical comedies at the turn of the twentieth century. Defined as a “decorative practice that playfully riffs on Oriental objects—Chinese or Japanese” (16), chinoiserie appears in the form of set designs and fantasies of geographical mobility and interracial heterosexual romance. Gilded, sensuous, and leisurely idyllic, the Orient in the musical comedy is representative of an alternative world to which any Westerner would want to belong, a cross-cultural utopia “where East and West can indeed meet with highly gratifying and festive results” (35). Through the chapter's analysis of operas and theatrical plays, Gan teases out a historical utopian impulse—the “wishful hope of universal and cross-cultural harmony” (35)—in the deployment of chinoiserie that peaked in the mid-eighteenth century. The resilience of these popular texts attests to a form of Sino-West relation that existed before the force of Western imperialism brought China to its doorstep and breached the fantasies of alterity.Rather than approaching Orientalist humor by contesting its misrepresentation of China, Gan argues that chinoiserie is “ultimately more revealing of the European self than the Chinese other” (16). Reading Ernest Bramah's Chinese fiction, which debuted at the onset of the anti-West Boxer Rebellion in China in 1900, chapter 2 illustrates the crucial transition between the nineteenth and twentieth centuries—a time period when the romantic chinoiserie disappeared and the Yellow Peril discourse arose. Focusing on Bramah, who had never set foot in China but was an assiduous collector of Chinese literature in translation, Gan traces the afterlife of literary chinoiserie in Bramah's fictional work, during a time when cross-cultural conflicts intensified, and highlights the resilient desire for interracial harmony as China became the object of fear. Through the Chinese storyteller Kai Lung, Bramah's Oriental China is presented as the radical other that is also comfortably familiar. His stories of adventures in an antiquated China do not take place in any particular historical period and depict a premodern world of splendor, poetry, and civilization, where “China” is turned into a space of Western nostalgia for a way of life that was disappearing in a rapidly modernizing world.In contrast to the distant encounter with romantic chinoiserie, the remainder of the book examines humor's role in literature written by Westerners who traveled to and resided in China. Through American missionary Authur Henderson Smith's infamous Chinese Characteristics (1890), chapter 3 probes the meaning of humor in a text known for its essentializing racial remarks. Complicating the Hobbesian thesis of superiority that interprets humor as a moment of “sudden glory,” Gan re-reads the frustrated humor in Chinese Characteristics as a record of Smith's way of “rewriting scenarios of vulnerability and bewilderment into ones of mastery and control” (69). Smith's text is presented not as a unique case but as an allegory of Westerners' challenged experience of alterity in China. However, as the influence of modern Western states on Chinese territories began to decline after the First World War, chapter 4 presents a selection of interwar travel writings, including the work of Peter Fleming and Christopher Isherwood, which show the waning sense of belonging to a superior culture and the embrace of their position as amateur travelers abroad. Instead of expressing uncertainty and humiliation, writings from the interwar era contain self-deprecating humor and the leveling of the self, signifying changing Sino-West relations that further developed into amicable humor among the new generation of writers who were long-term residents of China, especially in the treaty port of Shanghai. Reading the work of cartoonist Friedrich Schiff and writers Carl Crow and Emily Hahn, the last chapter traces the subtle transformation of humor and the imagination of cross-cultural friendship from a Chinese treaty port under Japanese invasion during the Second World War.“Humor can belittle and trivialize, but it can also humanize. It walks that knife-edge, teetering from lazy caricature to biting satire to companionable laughter” (133), Gan concludes. In this historical study of literary humor spanning fifty-five years where “China” is presented as a laughing matter, Gan warns against jumping to conclusions and argues for understanding humor as the desire to create common ground. The instances of humor and laughter in the book trace a meta-structure of feelings that are often misrecognized and disguised as Oriental fetishism. As China and the West came into intense and at times violent contact with each other, the emergence of literary humor across a variety of texts suggests a way of reading humor as a mode of managing the excessive and complex experience of cross-cultural encounters, rather than as a generic aesthetics. Emerging during a time when Western colonialism and the technologies of warfare and travel paralyzed the existing concepts of the self and the other, comedy is representative of a unique Anglo-American sentiment and a modern affective mode. Rather than interpreting the overlooked archive of popular culture according to the meta-discourse of Western colonialism in Asia, Comic China examines semi-colonial encounters from below, complicating and revealing the entangled relationships between the foreign and the self, and the semi-colonizer and the colonized.Gan's assertion that China is an anomaly within case studies of Orientalism is not necessarily contextualized in the unique history of semi-colonialism in China, where the Chinese state retained political sovereignty but ceded the control of its territories to foreign powers. However, the literary analyses emphasize Westerners' frustrations, anxieties, and especially the desire for cross-cultural harmony, opening up a micro-history of semi-colonial orientalism (lowercase)—and revealing entirely different affective histories that are not reducible to the meta-discourse of Orientalism (uppercase). The book's contribution lies in the discovery of laughter in creating the fluid conceptions of race and ethnicity, highlighting an underrepresented area of study in Sino-West relations.

## 1659. Integrating Artificial Intelligence and BIM in Construction: Systematic Review and Quantitative Comparative Analysis

- Authors: Reinaldo Valdebenito; Eric Forcael
- Year: 2025
- DOI: 10.3390/app152312470
- Venue: Applied Sciences
- Countries: CL
- Source: openalex
- URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/app152312470
- PDF: https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/15/23/12470/pdf?version=1764048538

In the transition toward a more digital and data-driven construction industry, understanding how Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Building Information Modeling (BIM) are integrated is key to planning, delivering, and operating projects effectively. This review examines recent studies to identify usage patterns of AI and BIM. Searches were conducted on the Web of Science Core Collection from 2022 to 2025. After running a reproducible review protocol aligned with PRISMA 2020, which began with 1212 articles, and after a funneling process, 12 studies met the predefined eligibility criteria. In the present study, the synthesis was non-meta-analytic; instead, the information was analyzed by using standardized tabulation with a consistent format and compared using a two-level weighting scheme. The methodological approach combines full-text reading and descriptive coding with a reproducible weighting scheme that accounts for mentions per study and integrates them at the corpus level using open-source tools. The results show a strong focus on Deep Learning (DL), with a greater presence in Digital Twins (DT) and BIM Modeling (BIMM); Multidimensional BIM (4D/5D) appears as a secondary line, while the Common Data Environment (CDE) and Clash detection (CD) are sporadic. The coupling of DL-DT and DL-BIMM predominates. Simultaneously, Machine Learning (ML) provides explainable analysis on structured data, and Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) and Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) with Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) act as enablers for data generation/adaptation and deployment with traceability. It is concluded that advancing metrics and shared datasets, especially for CDE and CD, along with developing reproducible workflows oriented toward MLOps, are key to scaling AI in real-world environments.

## 1660. Diffusion Models for Agricultural Imaging: A Systematic Review of Methods, Applications and Future Prospects

- Authors: Hewa Majeed Zangana; Shuai Li; Sharyar Wani
- Year: 2025
- DOI: 10.65500/agriculture-2025-003
- Venue: Impact in Agriculture
- Countries: FI; IQ; MY
- Source: openalex
- URL: https://doi.org/10.65500/agriculture-2025-003
- PDF: https://www.impaxon.com/journal/agriculture/assets/pdfs/agriculture-2025-003.pdf

Diffusion models are rapidly reshaping agricultural image analysis, offering high-fidelity synthetic data generation where real datasets are limited, imbalanced, or costly to collect. Traditional augmentation and GAN-based synthesis often struggle to preserve fine disease features and crop textures, leading to suboptimal model performance in real field conditions. This review consolidates the latest research on diffusion-based methods applied to plant disease diagnosis, fruit quality assessment, weed and pest monitoring, nematode identification, green-wall health evaluation, and UAV-based phenotyping. Reported literature demonstrates improved texture detail, lesion clarity, and better classification accuracy when diffusion-generated images supplement training datasets. Techniques such as latent diffusion and ControlNet enhance structure control, while text-guided models support domain transfer and unseen class synthesis. Despite promising outcomes, challenges remain concerning computational cost, real-world generalization across farms and seasons, and lack of standardized evaluation protocols. Future progress is expected through multimodal diffusion integrating hyperspectral and thermal inputs, efficient deployment on edge devices, and development of open benchmarks for comparative analysis. This review positions diffusion models as a leading generative approach for agricultural AI and outlines the research opportunities needed for practical adoption in large-scale farming environments.

## 1661. De Novo Drug Design using Artificial Intelligence ASYNT-GAN

- Authors: Ivan Jacobs; Manolis Μaragoudakis
- Year: 2020
- DOI: 10.20944/preprints202010.0196.v2
- Venue: Preprints.org
- Countries: GR
- Source: openalex
- URL: https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202010.0196.v2
- PDF: https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202010.0196/v2/download

In this paper we propose the generation of synthetic small and more sophisticated molecule structures that optimize the binding affinity to a target (ASYNT-GAN). To achieve this we leverage on three important achievements in A.I.: Attention, Deep Learning on Graphs and Generative Adversarial Networks. Similar to text generation based on parts of text we are able to generate a molecule architecture based on an existing target. By adopting this approach, we propose a novel way of searching for existing compounds that are suitable candidates. Similar to question and answer Natural Language solutions we are able to find drugs with highest relevance to a target. We are able to identify substructures of the molecular structure that are the most suitable for binding. In addition, we are proposing a novel way of generating the molecule in 3D space in such a way that the binding is optimized. We show that we are able to generate compound structures and protein structures that are optimised for binding to a target.

## 1662. Synthetic Tabular Data Generation Under Horizontal Federated Learning Environments in Acute Myeloid Leukemia: Case-Based Simulation Study

- Authors: Imanol Isasa; Mikel Catalina; Gorka Epelde; Naiara Aginako; Andoni Beristain
- Year: 2025
- DOI: 10.2196/74116
- Venue: JMIR Medical Informatics
- Countries: 
- Source: crossref
- URL: https://doi.org/10.2196/74116

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data scarcity and dispersion pose significant obstacles in biomedical research, particularly when addressing rare diseases. In such scenarios, synthetic data generation (SDG) has emerged as a promising path to mitigate the first issue. Concurrently, federated learning is a machine learning paradigm where multiple nodes collaborate to create a centralized model with knowledge that is distilled from the data in different nodes, but without the need for sharing it. This research explores the combination of SDG and federated learning technologies in the context of acute myeloid leukemia, a rare hematological disorder, evaluating their combined impact and the quality of the generated artificial datasets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to evaluate the privacy- and fidelity-related impact of horizontally federating SDG models in different data distribution scenarios and with different numbers of nodes, comparing them with centralized baseline SDG models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Two state-of-the-art generative models, conditional tabular generative adversarial network and FedTabDiff, were trained considering four different scenarios: (1) a nonfederated baseline with all the data available, (2) a federated scenario where the data were evenly distributed among different nodes, (3) a federated scenario where the data were unevenly and randomly distributed (imbalanced data), and (4) a federated scenario with nonindependent and identically distributed data distributions. For each of the federated scenarios, a fixed set of node quantities (3, 5, 7, 10) was considered to assess its impact, and the generated data were evaluated, attending to a fidelity-privacy trade-off.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The computed fidelity metrics exhibited statistically significant deteriorations (P&lt;.001) up to 21% in the conditional tabular generative adversarial network and up to 62% in the FedTabDiff model due to the federation process. When comparing federated experiments trained with diverse numbers of nodes, no strong tendencies were observed, even if specific comparisons resulted in significative differences. Privacy metrics were mainly maintained while obtaining maximum improvements of 55% and maximum deteriorations of 26% between both models, although they were not statistically significant.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Within the scope of the use case scenario in this paper, the act of horizontally federating SDG algorithms results in a loss of data fidelity compared to the nonfederated baseline while maintaining privacy levels. However, this deterioration does not significantly increase as the number of nodes used to train the models grows, even though significative differences were found in specific comparisons. The different data partition distribution configurations had no significant effect on the metrics, as similar tendencies were found for all scenarios.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
